units.title: Choose a test that can answer the baseball question
outcomes: Translate a baseball decision into a measurable construct and defensible outcome.
Distinguish validity, agreement, repeatability and utility.
Reject a metric whose inference exceeds its measurement.

body.heading: Start with the decision, not the device
body.text:
A test is useful when its result can change a decision that someone is authorized to make. Start with a concrete question: should the staff retain the current lower-body development emphasis over the next training block? Name the athlete group, time horizon and decision owner. Then identify the capacity or behavior that the test could inform. “Measure readiness” is too broad: readiness includes many interacting physical, psychological and contextual factors, and a single jump does not directly observe them all.

Separate four layers: the construct you care about, the task used to sample it, the measured signal, and the conclusion. A countermovement jump is a task. Vertical ground-reaction force is a signal. Jump height estimated from that signal is an outcome. The player’s capacity to repeat effective baseball actions is a broader construct. Moving between layers requires evidence and explicit assumptions, not a more impressive dashboard label.

body.heading: Write the inference you intend to defend
body.text:
An operational definition tells another practitioner what the number actually means. “Best hands-on-hips CMJ height, estimated by impulse–momentum from three valid trials” differs from “mean flight-time height during arm-swing jumps.” Both may be recorded in centimeters while measuring different versions of the task. The unit alone does not establish comparability.

For each proposed metric, finish two sentences: “This result directly describes…” and “This result may inform…, provided that…”. For jump height, the first sentence concerns the performed jump under the recorded conditions. The second might concern a longitudinal development discussion, provided testing is comparable and uncertainty is considered. It should not automatically concern tissue health, injury probability, mechanical power, or permission to play. Write the unsupported inferences beside the supported ones so the limits survive transfer between staff.

body.heading: Validity belongs to a use and context
body.text:
Criterion evidence compares a measurement with an appropriate reference method. Construct evidence examines whether the measure behaves in ways expected from a defensible account of the underlying attribute. Neither is a permanent stamp attached to a brand. A device may estimate jump height acceptably for one movement but perform differently for a rapid landing metric. A test may distinguish widely separated groups yet fail to resolve a small within-player change.

Ask whether the study population, instructions, device version, outcome definition and measurement range resemble your planned use. An experiment in physically active adults can support a measurement principle without establishing a professional-baseball threshold. Read methods before borrowing conclusions. A baseball badge on a product page cannot replace a protocol comparison, and a general textbook cannot demonstrate that your own collection process is accurate.

body.heading: Association cannot demonstrate interchangeability
body.text:
Imagine two fictional systems measuring the same three trials. System A reports 30,40,50 cm; system B reports 35,45,55 cm. Their rank order is identical and their Pearson correlation is 1, yet B is 5 cm higher for every trial. A coach comparing yesterday’s A result with today’s B result could invent a training gain that never occurred.

Agreement asks about these differences: their direction, size and variation across the measurement range. Before testing a replacement system, agree what disagreement would matter for the intended decision. Report differences in useful units and inspect individual observations. A statistically nonsignificant mean difference does not prove that two systems agree closely enough; small samples can provide imprecise estimates. Conversely, a tiny precisely estimated difference can be statistically detectable while irrelevant to the practical decision.

body.heading: Reliability is necessary, but an unchanging number can still be useless
body.text:
Repeatability means that repeated measurements under the defined conditions produce sufficiently consistent results. A broken scale that always returns the same value is consistent but does not measure meaningful change. Similarly, athletes can learn to give the same questionnaire answer to avoid follow-up. Low variation must therefore be interpreted alongside validity, collection behavior and the question being asked.

The cost of a test includes athlete effort, disruption of baseball work, setup, analysis and the consequences of a misleading result. A precise maximal test performed at a poorly chosen time may cost more than its information is worth. A less elaborate measure can be preferable when it answers the actual question with acceptable uncertainty. Specify what you would do with a higher result, a lower result, an ambiguous result and no valid result before requesting athlete time.

body.heading: Build a small battery with a clear ownership map
body.text:
For a fictional position-player development review, a small battery might sample a lower-body task, acceleration performance and relevant baseball exposure. Each addresses a different question. Redundant metrics from one jump do not automatically create independent evidence; they may share the same raw signal and processing error. Prefer a short list of interpretable outcomes over dozens of correlated flags.

Document who collects, checks, interprets and acts. The performance scientist owns measurement quality and its explanation. S&C and baseball staff integrate the result with training and skill priorities. Clinical symptoms or restrictions remain with the appropriate medical team. Disagreement among these inputs is a reason to investigate context. It is not permission to average them into a universal readiness score whose weighting and consequences have never been validated.

body.heading: Read a methods section with a decision worksheet
body.text:
When reading a study, make a compact extraction table rather than highlighting only the conclusion. Record the sample, test version, device, operator structure, timing, number of valid trials, summary metric, error estimate and its uncertainty. Then add a final column: “What changes in our setting?” This makes transfer limits visible before the study becomes a departmental rule.

Use the Souza CMJ paper as a short appraisal exercise: it concerns active adult men and a specified protocol, and reliability differs by metric. Its usefulness is showing why one test can produce outcomes of unequal repeatability. It does not provide an error value for every professional-baseball affiliate. Your proposed application should identify which methodological features you can reproduce and which require new local evidence.

units.title: Standardize the session: calibration, instructions and metadata
outcomes: Write a reproducible collection procedure with explicit stop and invalid-trial rules.
Distinguish zeroing, checking and calibration.
Preserve enough metadata to reconstruct a measurement.

body.heading: A number is the end of a collection chain
body.text:
Consider two reported jumps of 40 cm. One followed a familiar warm-up on the usual platform before training. The other followed a long bus trip, used a different operator and allowed arm swing. The same value does not establish the same performance state. Metadata describes the chain that generated each observation so that comparisons can be judged rather than assumed.

Define session identifiers, athlete identifiers, date and local time with time-zone handling, protocol version, device serial number, software and firmware, operator, task instructions, trial sequence, units and aggregation. Include relevant context such as preceding training and deviations from the intended procedure. Keep identifiers stable when an athlete changes affiliate; team names and names alone are unreliable join keys. Collect sensitive context only when needed, authorized and appropriately protected.

body.heading: Zeroing is not a full calibration
body.text:
Zeroing or taring establishes the current unloaded reference according to the device’s procedure. A functional check tests whether the device behaves as expected under known conditions. Calibration establishes the relationship between readings and known reference quantities, with procedures and tolerances appropriate to the instrument. These activities are related but not interchangeable. Do not call an empty-platform zero a complete verification of accuracy across the force range.

Follow the actual manufacturer’s setup, warm-up, mounting, capacity and maintenance instructions. A classroom diagram cannot supply the correct calibration procedure for every model. Record when and by whom checks were completed, the reference used, readings, acceptance rule and corrective action. An unexplained discrepancy is a reason to pause affected collection and investigate. Silently subtracting an offset after seeing athlete results can conceal an unresolved instrument problem.

body.heading: Standardize the task without confusing uniformity with realism
body.text:
Write the warm-up, footwear and surface requirements, permitted movement, start position, instructions, rest and trial count. Teach the task before using it to evaluate training. Familiarization helps reduce learning-related differences, but the number of sessions required is athlete- and task-dependent. A universal familiarization dose is not established by this course.

Decide which features must remain fixed and which can vary within the protocol. For example, allowing self-selected countermovement depth may be deliberate, but changing from fixed to self-selected depth halfway through a series changes the measurement context. Record the decision. Use the same encouragement script and feedback policy. If the purpose is monitoring under routine field conditions, estimate reliability under those conditions instead of claiming that ideal laboratory repeatability automatically transfers to travel-heavy baseball operations.

body.heading: Define an invalid trial before you see the score
body.text:
An invalid trial violates a measurement rule: stepping off a platform, an equipment dropout, a false gate trigger, or an unauthorized movement under that protocol. A low result can be perfectly valid. Write rejection criteria before collection and retain rejected trials with reasons. This prevents selective deletion of inconvenient observations and preserves the ability to audit a surprising report.

A synthetic session contains three CMJ estimates:38.0,41.0 and 40.0 cm. Video shows the 41.0 cm trial used arm swing despite a hands-on-hips rule. If the SOP requires the mean of three valid trials, you do not average the remaining two and pretend the requirement was met. Follow the predeclared replacement or incomplete-session rule. If a safe replacement produces 39.0 cm, the valid mean is 39.0 cm. The rejected value remains in the raw record.

body.heading: Aggregation is part of the outcome definition
body.text:
The best trial, mean of all valid trials and median answer different questions and respond differently to noise. Choose one because it matches the intended use, then estimate reliability for that exact summary. A best-of-five estimate is not interchangeable with a mean-of-three estimate. More attempts create more opportunities for an extreme result and may also introduce fatigue or learning.

Keep trial-level data even when the dashboard displays one number. Store validity, order and reason codes separately from the value. A displayed session average must be traceable to the exact included trials. Avoid rounding before aggregation or uncertainty calculations; round for communication at the end. Report precision consistent with the method. A software export containing six decimals does not demonstrate six-decimal accuracy or justify interpreting tiny fluctuations.

body.heading: Version changes need a bridge, not a hidden edit
body.text:
Suppose a new software release changes movement-onset detection. Archive the previous procedure, document the release and determine which metrics could change. Where feasible, process the same retained raw traces using both versions. This paired comparison helps separate algorithm differences from athlete change, although it cannot validate parts of the collection chain that also changed.

If comparable reprocessing is impossible, mark a break in the longitudinal record and collect a new baseline under the revised method. Explain what can and cannot be compared. For device replacement, a planned overlap study may be needed, subject to staff expertise and athlete burden. Do not blend two methods into one trend line merely because the column names match. A good SOP includes ownership of revisions, a version date and a process for staff training.

body.heading: Make the instructions understandable to the athlete
body.text:
Standardization depends on shared understanding, not simply reading identical words. Check that the athlete understands the task, the requested effort and the reason for repeating it. If instructions are delivered in more than one language, agree a consistent translation and demonstration with qualified staff, and document meaningful changes. A memorized script that the athlete interprets differently is not a standardized procedure.

Record whether feedback is given after each trial or only after the session. Competitive feedback can change behavior and may be an intentional feature, but it should not appear unpredictably. Use a brief teach-back or demonstration during familiarization. If the athlete misunderstands today’s task, correct the instruction and apply the established trial policy; do not interpret the resulting discrepancy as lost physical capacity.

body.heading: The instrument does not observe every quantity on the report
body.text:
A force plate measures forces, and depending on its design also moments, through a calibrated sensing system. Many displayed outputs are subsequently calculated. Vertical center-of-mass acceleration requires a force balance and an estimate of body mass. Velocity requires integration and an initial condition. Jump height requires further assumptions. The chain matters because an error at an early step can affect several apparently separate metrics.

For a stationary 80 kg athlete usingg = 9.81 m/s², expected vertical support force is approximately 784.8 N. During a fictional instant with vertical ground-reaction force 1,200 N, net vertical force is 1,200 − 784.8 = 415.2 N, giving upward acceleration 415.2/80 = 5.19 m/s². The 1,200 N reading is not itself net force. With two platforms under separate feet, use the appropriately synchronized total vertical force for whole-body acceleration, not one side alone.

body.heading: Force, impulse and power answer different questions
body.text:
Force describes interaction at an instant; impulse integrates net force over time and changes momentum. Power is a rate of mechanical energy transfer and depends on the specified force and corresponding velocity. Multiplying a reported peak force by a peak velocity measured at a different instant does not generally yield true peak power. The maxima may occur at different times.

For a deliberately simple synthetic interval, constant net upward force 200 N applied for 0.20 s produces 40 N·s of net impulse. For an 80 kg system initially at rest, the associated velocity change is 40/80 = 0.50 m/s. This arithmetic is a small segment example, not an entire jump. Real movement requires the whole relevant trace, signed force, an appropriate integration method and valid initial conditions. An impressive peak alone cannot explain how the athlete accumulated velocity across the movement.

body.heading: Dynamometry: respect the lever arm and the setup
body.text:
A dynamometer reading in newtons describes a force at the contact point. External joint torque requires the perpendicular moment arm: torque = force × perpendicular distance. In a synthetic example,200 N applied with a 0.30 m perpendicular moment arm corresponds to 60 N·m. The same 200 N at 0.25 m corresponds to 50 N·m. Comparing force alone while changing placement can therefore misrepresent the mechanical comparison.

Document joint angle, body position, stabilization, device placement, contraction instruction and duration, side, rest and operator. A handheld setup can be limited by examiner capacity or stabilization. A fixed apparatus introduces its own alignment and setup requirements. Do not equate measured external torque with the force in one muscle or with tissue load. Multiple muscles and passive structures can contribute, and the calculation does not solve their individual contributions.

body.heading: Timing systems measure an interval defined by events
body.text:
A timing result is the time between specified trigger events. Gate position, beam height, start procedure, athlete distance behind the first gate and the body part that breaks the beam can change that interval. A standing-start 10 m time and a flying 10 m time do not answer the same performance question. A stopwatch adds human event-detection error and should not silently replace an electronic system in a longitudinal series.

If a fictional 10 m interval takes 1.50 s, average speed over that interval is 10/1.50 ≈ 6.67 m/s. This is not maximum instantaneous speed. A runner could accelerate throughout the interval. If the question concerns acceleration from a baseball start, reproduce and document the start task; if it concerns peak-speed exposure, choose a method capable of addressing that different question. Surface, footwear and wind conditions belong in the comparison.

body.heading: Choose the metric before choosing the shopping list
body.text:
A resource-limited affiliate can still conduct disciplined testing. Start with the question, available method and meaningful resolution. A simpler test with transparent procedures can support a limited conclusion. It cannot be made equivalent to a laboratory measurement merely by renaming its output. Likewise, expensive hardware does not remove a poorly chosen task, an inconsistent operator or a weak interpretation.

Build an instrument specification sheet: what is sensed directly, what is derived, required units, relevant measurement range, sampling or timing resolution, access to raw data, processing transparency, known validation evidence and local operating constraints. Ask vendors to define proprietary terms. If the method is undisclosed, state what cannot be independently reconstructed and decide whether the remaining information is sufficient for the intended use. Treat procurement and measurement design as connected decisions.

body.heading: Testing technique is a practical skill that needs observation
body.text:
Reading the procedure and calculating the examples prepare you for practical work. They do not verify that you can align a sensor, identify a false trigger, coach a repeatable effort or stop an inappropriate test. The course project therefore separates a documented simulation from an observed collection. Keep an honest evidence log: source reviewed, mock setup rehearsed, supervised session completed and feedback acted upon.

Before working with athletes, obtain the appropriate organizational permission and supervision, explain the purpose and burden, and respect existing restrictions. Do not add maximal tests to a rehabilitation plan without the responsible team’s authorization. When equipment is unavailable, work from synthetic traces and critique demonstration footage or a mock SOP. Record the missing practical competency rather than turning a paper exercise into a claim of real-device competence.

body.heading: An asymmetry percentage needs a denominator and a task
body.text:
Two hypothetical unilateral forces of 900 N and 1,000 N differ by 100 N. Dividing by the larger value gives 10%; dividing by their mean 950 N gives approximately 10.53%. Both are possible formulas, but they are not identical and should not share an unexplained “asymmetry” label. Record the equation and which side is higher, not just the magnitude.

A side difference in one test does not locate an injured tissue or establish a dangerous threshold. Side dominance, movement strategy, setup and measurement error can contribute, and a bilateral task does not automatically isolate unilateral capacity. Check whether the direction persists across comparable observations and whether the result matters for the named task. Do not prescribe a correction solely because one percentage exceeds a generic number from a different test.

body.heading: A sampled signal is a sequence, not continuous truth
body.text:
A digital recording samples a physical signal at discrete times. At 1,000 Hz the nominal interval is 0.001 s; at 100 Hz it is 0.01 s. The latter offers fewer observations of rapid changes, but a high advertised sample rate alone does not guarantee an accurate measurement. Sensor behavior, analog conditioning, synchronization, resolution and processing also matter. Confirm what the exported rate represents and whether samples were resampled or averaged.

Check timestamps rather than assuming the requested rate was achieved without gaps. A missing segment is not a string of zero-force observations. A zero-filled gap can create false event boundaries and distort integration. Record whether data were lost, interpolated or excluded, and why. Sampling requirements should be justified for the metric and instrument; this lesson does not prescribe one universal frequency for every sport-science application.

body.heading: Filtering trades noise reduction against signal detail
body.text:
A filter changes the frequency content of a signal. Smoothing can reduce unwanted fluctuations, but it can also change peaks, slopes and event timing. The result depends on filter type, order, cutoff, implementation and boundary handling. A visually smooth curve is not automatically more valid. Preserve the original acquisition export and create a separately versioned processed copy.

The Sahrom study provides a documented example of selecting and reporting processing methods for a particular CMJ investigation. Its settings are study methods, not a recipe to paste into every platform. For your own workflow, ask what noise is being removed, what real behavior could be attenuated, and whether the method has been evaluated for the target metric. A proprietary export labeled “raw” may already contain internal processing; document that uncertainty rather than claiming access to untouched sensor data.

body.heading: Find events with a definition that can be checked
body.text:
Movement onset, minimum velocity, the transition from downward to upward motion, takeoff and landing are different events. A force threshold may be used in an algorithm, but its definition must be explicit: reference baseline, threshold direction, duration requirement, search window and handling of noise. Review detected events against plausible traces, not only against the final number.

During a CMJ with upward defined as positive, downward center-of-mass velocity can coexist with upward acceleration. That is braking: motion remains downward while the force balance is slowing it. The lowest center-of-mass position occurs when vertical velocity crosses from negative to positive, not necessarily at the highest force. Confusing force, acceleration and velocity signs can shift phase boundaries and alter the impulse or duration attributed to each phase.

body.heading: Integration accumulates both signal and error
body.text:
For vertical motion, subtract body weight from support force and divide by mass to estimate acceleration. Integrating acceleration gives change in velocity; an initial velocity must be supplied. In a quiet-standing start, zero initial vertical velocity is a reasonable model assumption if the athlete was actually stationary. Integrating velocity then gives displacement relative to an initial position. Small baseline errors can accumulate across these steps.

In a synthetic example, an unrecognized 8 N net-force offset for an 80 kg athlete adds 0.10 m/s² acceleration. Across 0.50 s it adds 0.05 m/s of velocity error under constant-offset assumptions. That error then affects subsequent calculations. The example explains sensitivity, not a universal allowable offset. Quiet-standing quality, mass estimation, the integration window and the actual force baseline must therefore be inspected together.

body.heading: Different height calculations have different assumptions
body.text:
Impulse–momentum estimation uses takeoff velocity and the ballistic relationshiph = v²/(2g) to estimate center-of-mass rise after takeoff, assuming flight is governed by gravity. With synthetic takeoff velocity 2.50 m/s andg = 9.81 m/s², h = 6.25/19.62 ≈ 0.319 m. This is not automatically total center-of-mass displacement from quiet standing to the apex; pre-takeoff movement changes the reference position.

Flight-time estimation commonly usesh = gt²/8 under the assumption that center-of-mass height at landing equals that at takeoff. Altered landing posture can violate this assumption. Do not compare a flight-time estimate with an impulse–momentum estimate as though changing the equation cannot change the result. Identify which height is reported, its reference point, the detected events and the assumptions. Neither equation by itself establishes the player’s readiness or the cause of a change.

body.heading: A processing comparison is an experiment on the pipeline
body.text:
Suppose the same stored traces produce a fictional mean height 40.0 cm with processing versionA and 41.2 cm with versionB. Because the athletes did not repeat the jumps, the 1.2 cm difference is a processing difference, not new adaptation. Inspect per-trial differences and the events that changed. The average alone may conceal larger disagreements on unusual trials.

Lock the chosen method for a comparison period where feasible. If revision is warranted, retain both versions, document the reason and assess whether historical data can be reprocessed consistently. Do not choose settings simply because they produce the desired training story. Your audit should include an anomalous trace, a missing-data example and a normal trace. A second analyst should be able to reproduce the same output from the same input and named settings.

body.heading: Audit time before integrating anything
body.text:
A deliberately tiny exported sequence has timestamps 0.000,0.001,0.002 and 0.010 s. The first gaps are 1 ms, but the last is 8 ms. Treating all four points as evenly spaced 1 ms observations would misrepresent elapsed time. The correct response is to inspect the acquisition record, determine whether samples are missing and apply a documented rule appropriate to the analysis. The sequence is a diagnostic toy, not a usable jump trace.

Also inspect clipping: a flat top at the instrument’s range limit may indicate saturation rather than a genuine force plateau. Interpolation or smoothing cannot reconstruct information that the sensor never recorded with acceptable certainty. Flag the affected metric, preserve the trace and explain what is unavailable. A plausible-looking final curve does not excuse an undocumented repair.

body.heading: Decide what you want to generalize
body.text:
A reliability study is a design problem before it is a calculation. Repeating trials within one session answers a narrower question than repeating sessions on different days. Using the same operator does not estimate the additional variation introduced by different operators. Testing one platform does not establish agreement among every platform in an organization. Write the intended future use first, then reproduce the relevant variations in the study.

For an affiliate dashboard using the mean of three valid CMJs collected by rotating staff, a useful design should address the session summary and the staff workflow. Three trials by one expert in a quiet laboratory cannot fully represent that deployment. You may begin with a controlled pilot to locate technical problems, then test the intended field process. Label each stage and avoid presenting a narrow pilot as a completed organization-wide reliability evaluation.

body.heading: Choose an interval that avoids both carryover and real change
body.text:
If sessions are too close, residual fatigue, practice or memory can influence the retest. If they are too far apart, true training adaptation, detraining or clinical change may occur. There is no universal interval that solves this for every test. Choose and justify the timing based on task burden, athlete experience and the operating context, while recording intervening activity.

A study designed to estimate short-term measurement repeatability should aim for a sufficiently stable underlying attribute across observations. Stability cannot simply be declared because the calendar interval looks reasonable. Inspect symptoms, training, travel and protocol deviations that could challenge it. Excluding every inconvenient real-world condition can produce an estimate too optimistic for routine use; including major true changes can make an instrument appear noisier than it is. State which question your design addresses.

body.heading: Bias and scatter are different features
body.text:
For each athlete, calculate retest minus baseline using one consistent sign convention. The average difference estimates the systematic shift between occasions in that sample. The spread of differences reflects random disagreement around that shift, plus any unmodeled true changes. If everyone gains 2 cm after learning the task, average bias is 2 cm; a method that ignores this shift can overstate comparability.

Use a paired table and a difference-versus-mean plot. The horizontal coordinate is the average of each pair; the vertical coordinate is retest−baseline. Look for a common offset, increasing spread at larger values, unusual observations and subgroups. A single summary coefficient can conceal these patterns. Investigate an unusual point through the raw record and prespecified rules; do not delete it simply because it weakens the desired reliability result.

body.heading: Work through paired differences by hand
body.text:
Five synthetic athlete differences are−1,0,1,2,3 cm. Mean difference is 1 cm. Deviations from that mean are−2,−1,0,1,2 cm; their squared sum is 10 cm². Using the sample denominatorn−1 = 4, the difference variance is 2.5 cm² and SD is√2.5 ≈ 1.581 cm. Under a stable-trait, equal independent error model, typical error isSD of differences/√2 ≈ 1.118 cm.

The 1 cm shift and 1.118 cm random-error estimate answer different questions and should both be reported. Approximate 95% limits of agreement are mean difference ± 1.96 × SD of differences, here 1 ± 3.099 cm, or about−2.10 to 4.10 cm. These describe a model of individual between-session differences, not the confidence interval for the mean bias. Five invented pairs illustrate arithmetic; they do not provide a sufficiently precise estimate for professional decisions.

body.heading: Inspect whether error grows with the size of the measure
body.text:
Absolute differences can be larger in stronger or higher-performing athletes simply because variability scales with the size of the measure. This is heteroscedasticity: the spread is not constant across the measurement range. A single error expressed in newtons may then describe small and large readings unequally. Plot the data before deciding whether an absolute or proportional model is appropriate.

For positive ratio-scale outcomes, log transformation can help model proportional error when the pattern supports it. Differences on the log scale represent ratios after back-transformation. Do not apply logarithms to zero or negative values, and do not introduce an arbitrary constant simply to make an inconvenient dataset fit. If residual behavior remains problematic or the sample is tiny, state the limitation and seek statistical review. A transformation does not repair protocol mixing, data entry errors or missing observations.

body.heading: Report the design as carefully as the coefficient
body.text:
Describe the athlete sample, selection, task, device, operators, repetitions, interval, conditions, aggregation, exclusions and uncertainty. Report how many participants provided complete pairs and why others did not. Missing retests may be informative: the players unavailable because of symptoms or travel may differ from those with complete data. An error estimate from only the easiest-to-test athletes may not represent the full operational setting.

Plan sample size around desired precision and the analysis, with appropriate statistical support. Do not invent a universal minimum number. Distinguish an early feasibility pilot from a definitive estimate. Preserve trial-level and session-level tables, code or formulas, and plots. A competent reader should understand what varied, what was held constant and which future measurements the result can reasonably inform. Reliability is a property of measurements under a process, not a timeless property of a device name.

body.heading: Keep technical and biological repeatability distinct
body.text:
Repeated analysis of the identical stored trace can test processing reproducibility but contains no new athlete effort. Repeated jumps within a visit add execution variability. Repeating the visit adds more possible variation from context and biology. These nested questions can be investigated in stages to locate a problem efficiently.

For example, if two analysts produce different numbers from identical raw input and nominally identical settings, first resolve the processing discrepancy. Asking athletes to repeat the test will not fix that software or procedure issue. If analysis agrees but session summaries vary, inspect execution and context. This staged approach helps direct limited athlete time toward the uncertainty that remains. Report exactly which layer has been evaluated and avoid calling every form of repetition “test–retest reliability.”

body.heading: Use a family of statistics, not one reliability badge
body.text:
Relative reliability concerns separation among people compared with unwanted variation. Absolute error concerns the size of uncertainty in the original measurement units or a justified proportional scale. A broad sample can retain clear rank differences despite error too large for a subtle within-player decision. A homogeneous elite group can have a modest ICC even when absolute error is small. Report both perspectives and the sample context.

In a simplified variance illustration with no systematic bias, between-athlete variance 100 and error variance 4 yield 100/(100+4) ≈ 0.962. If the between-athlete variance is 4 with the same error variance 4, the ratio becomes 0.50. The measurement error has not improved or worsened between these constructed examples; the population spread changed. This ratio is a conceptual illustration, not a substitute for fitting the correct ICC to real repeated measurements.

body.heading: State the ICC question in words
body.text:
An ICC report should identify its model, agreement definition, score type, software and confidence interval. Are the same operators used for everyone? Are conclusions restricted to those operators or generalized more broadly? Does the application use one measurement or an average of several? Must readings agree numerically, or is a consistent offset acceptable? These choices precede interpretation.

Koo and Li’s selected reporting guidance distinguishes model, single-versus-average type, and absolute agreement versus consistency. Liljequist and colleagues show why agreement and consistency can diverge when systematic shifts occur. For this course, write the intended interpretation before selecting software options. Do not copy an ICC label from another paper without checking its notation. A negative sample estimate is possible and is not “negative measurement error”; investigate the design and uncertainty rather than silently converting it into a favorable value.

body.heading: Typical error from repeated pairs
body.text:
With two comparable occasions and a stable underlying quantity, letd = follow-up−baseline for each participant. The sample SD ofd describes the variation of paired differences around their average. If occasion errors are independent and have equal variance, variance of the difference is twice the single-measurement error variance. Therefore typical error = SD(d)/√2. State the systematic mean difference separately.

For the earlier synthetic differences−1,0,1,2,3 cm, SD(d) = 1.581 cm and typical error ≈ 1.118 cm. It does not follow that every result is exactly 1.118 cm wrong. The statistic describes a model of variation in the population and conditions studied. If the trait changes between sessions, errors correlate, or variability differs across occasions, the simple model needs revision. Repeating the formula cannot rescue an unsuitable design.

body.heading: SEM has a specific measurement meaning here
body.text:
SEM in this course means standard error of measurement: an estimate of the random spread around a person’s underlying score under a specified measurement model. It is not the standard error of a sample mean, often calculated asSD/√n to describe precision of a group mean. These answer different questions. Increasing the number of athletes improves estimation precision; it does not by itself make an individual measurement less noisy.

A common classical expression isSEM = SD × √(1−reliability), but the SD and reliability coefficient must come from compatible variance definitions and the intended design. Incompatible combinations can produce a misleading number. A residual error estimate from an appropriate model may be more direct. Typical error and measurement SEM can coincide under the same simple error model, but the names alone do not guarantee identical estimands. Always state how your error estimate was obtained.

body.heading: CV describes relative variation only when its scale makes sense
body.text:
For a positive ratio-scale outcome, a simple coefficient of variation is 100 × SD/mean, expressed as a percentage. In a reliability context, specify whether the numerator is a within-person error estimate or an ordinary SD across observations. A between-athlete SD divided by the team mean describes team dispersion; it is not automatically measurement error. The denominator and analysis scale matter.

Using a synthetic error estimate 1.0 cm around a 40 cm reference mean gives an approximate relative error of 2.5%. Around 20 cm the same absolute 1.0 cm is 5%. This illustrates why units and scale should remain visible. Ratios become unstable near zero and can be meaningless for scales without a meaningful zero. When a log-scale model is justified, back-transform with the model-appropriate expression and document it; do not mix arithmetic and log-derived CV values as though they were computed identically.

body.heading: Detectable change combines error from both measurements
body.text:
For two independent measurements with equal SEM and approximately normal random error, the standard deviation of their difference is√2 × SEM. A conventional two-sided 95% detectable-change margin is 1.96 × √2 × SEM, approximately 2.77 × SEM. WithSEM1.0 cm, that margin is 2.77 cm. A change from 40 to 43 cm is+3 cm; its approximate measurement-error interval is 3 ± 2.77 cm, or 0.23 to 5.77 cm, if bias is negligible and the model holds.

A change from 40 to 42 cm gives 2 ± 2.77 cm, or−0.77 to 4.77 cm. Crossing zero means these observations do not resolve the direction under this error model; it does not prove no adaptation. Exceeding the margin does not prove training caused the change or that it matters in baseball. The margin is a statement about measurement detectability under assumptions, not a readiness, injury or clearance threshold.

body.heading: When the simple difference formula no longer fits
body.text:
If baseline and follow-up errors have different standard deviations, the independent-error standard deviation of their difference is√(SEMbaseline²+SEMfollow-up²), not automatically√2 times either one. With synthetic errors 1 and 2 cm, it is√5 ≈ 2.236 cm, giving a conventional 95% margin of about 4.383 cm. The equal-error shortcut would be inappropriate.

If errors are correlated, the variance of the difference additionally includes−2 × covariance. This is why shared calibration errors and repeated measurements need an explicit model. Do not estimate covariance from one athlete pair or choose an assumption because it produces the desired answer. These extensions illustrate the design logic; the built-in explorer uses the simpler equal-independent-error model. For complex data, obtain a statistically reviewed analysis that matches the collection design.

body.heading: Three questions sit beside every before-and-after difference
body.text:
First, how large is the observed change relative to the measurement process? Second, is a change of that size important for the decision? Third, what caused it? These are different questions. A highly detectable change can be too small to matter; a potentially worthwhile change can be hidden within uncertainty; and either can occur for reasons unrelated to the training program under discussion.

Define practical importance before seeing the result where possible. It may depend on the athlete’s task, performance needs, cost and decision consequences. A generic fraction of the team SD is a distribution-based convention, not automatic evidence of what matters to one professional player. Discuss the proposed worthwhile threshold with relevant staff and document the rationale. Do not let a convenient statistical formula silently become the organization’s performance philosophy.

body.heading: Compare an uncertainty interval with the decision boundary
body.text:
Consider a synthetic CMJ change from 40 to 43 cm, with compatible measurement SEM1 cm and negligible bias. The conventional two-measurement error margin is 2.77 cm; the approximate interval is 0.23 to 5.77 cm. Under those assumptions, the pair resolves a positive direction at this margin. Suppose the staff had provisionally defined 2 cm as the smallest change that would justify revising a development emphasis. The interval includes values both below and above 2 cm, so practical importance is still unresolved.

The 2 cm boundary is an invented teaching choice, not a validated baseball threshold. Display its rationale and uncertainty separately from measurement error. Do not report that the player has a particular probability of being improved from this simple calculation. The interval here is a frequentist-style measurement-error approximation with an externally supplied error estimate, not a fully specified Bayesian probability model or a complete model of all biological variation.

body.heading: Choose an action by its consequences as well as the estimate
body.text:
A measurement can justify a conversation or a low-cost reversible adjustment without supporting a high-stakes restriction. Compare the consequence of acting when no important change occurred with the consequence of failing to act when one did. The acceptable evidence may differ for scheduling an extra review, revising an eight-week development plan and making a clinical availability decision.

Write an action rule with a named owner: validate the observation, gather specific context, compare complementary evidence, select an authorized action and record a follow-up. Avoid converting every amber result into less training; repeated automatic reductions can become an unexamined intervention. Conversely, a normal score should not override a concerning symptom report. Medical concerns go through the appropriate clinical process rather than being averaged against a favorable jump metric.

body.heading: Repeated observations can help, but dependence matters
body.text:
Additional observations can reduce uncertainty when they are relevant and collected under a suitable design. Averaging independent errors reduces their variance, but repeated trials can share the same device offset, warm-up, motivation or fatigue. Closely spaced observations may therefore be correlated. ApplyingSEM/√k automatically to every set of repeated results can overstate the gain in precision.

Estimate reliability for the actual summary used in practice. If you adopt a mean-of-three session metric, evaluate that summary rather than recycling the error for one trial. For repeated days, consider genuine day-to-day changes as well as technical noise. Collect more data only when it can change the decision and its burden is justified. A second test requested merely to obtain a preferred answer introduces selection and can make the process less trustworthy.

body.heading: Baseball context explains what the metric cannot
body.text:
A decline after overnight travel may reflect altered sleep, testing time, warm-up or other factors, but the sequence alone does not prove which mechanism caused it. Record these plausible explanations and seek the information that could distinguish them. An unchanged jump after a large throwing exposure does not demonstrate that the elbow has recovered. The measured task and the tissue-specific question are different.

Use a short evidence table: observation, collection quality, uncertainty, relevant context and unresolved alternatives. Give contextual information a traceable role rather than using it to rationalize any preferred conclusion. When different inputs disagree, state the disagreement. A coach may provide a task-specific observation that the sensor cannot detect, while the measurement may challenge an impression that deserves checking. Integration is a structured discussion, not an unvalidated weighted average.

body.heading: Finish with a report the next person can act on
body.text:
Lead with the observation and its limit: “The session mean increased 3 cm; under our current error model the direction is clearer than the practical importance.” Add the intended action, responsible person and next evidence needed. Keep the raw number, uncertainty and protocol version available for technical review. A short coach-facing message and a detailed methods appendix can express the same conclusion at different resolutions.

Then ask the receiver to explain the next step in their own words. If they hear “below the threshold” as “nothing happened,” correct that interpretation. If they hear “detectable” as “safe to play,” correct it immediately. Log the action actually taken and the subsequent observation so the measurement process can be evaluated. A dashboard that is never connected to a documented decision cannot demonstrate that it improves practice.

body.heading: Avoid a search for whichever metric changes most
body.text:
A platform may produce dozens of correlated outputs. Inspecting every one and highlighting only the largest favorable change creates a selective story. Decide the primary outcome and a small number of supporting outcomes before reviewing the block where possible. Retain the complete agreed report and label unplanned findings as exploratory.

This does not mean ignoring an unexpected pattern. It means distinguishing a new question from a confirmed conclusion. Verify the underlying trace and processing, consider the number of metrics inspected and seek a relevant follow-up. If a surprising phase metric changes while the primary outcome remains stable, explain that both can occur and that the finding needs interpretation. Do not upgrade an exploratory signal into proof that the athlete needs a specific exercise.

body.heading: Your final product is a reproducible decision process
body.text:
The course ends with an operational package, not a score copied from a calculator. Another trained person should be able to understand the question, repeat the collection procedure, reconstruct the analysis and see why the proposed action follows. Choose one test that your resources can support. A carefully executed modest project is stronger than a complex device portfolio with no traceable methods.

State the athlete role and decision: for example, reviewing a lower-body development emphasis for an outfielder over a defined block. Separate the proposed testing question from any medical clearance question. List prerequisites for collection, including organizational permission, participant explanation, equipment competence and applicable restrictions. If you cannot meet them, conduct the supplied-data simulation and mark practical observation pending. The written work remains valuable without overstating what it demonstrates.

body.heading: Write the SOP and rehearse the failure cases
body.text:
Your SOP should cover setup and checks, task instruction, familiarization, trial count, rest, validity rules, replacement policy, termination process and aggregation. Include the data dictionary and a setup diagram. A concise document can be complete if its terms are precise. “Perform a normal warm-up” is not reproducible; identify the sequence and the allowed individual adjustments.

Rehearse what happens when a device fails, an athlete cannot complete the task, a trial is invalid, a collector changes or a symptom is reported. Do not improvise the policy after seeing a result. Assign who can stop collection and who resolves uncertainty. Test the instructions with a colleague using a mock session. Their questions reveal hidden assumptions that a polished document may conceal. Record the revision rather than presenting the first draft as final.

body.heading: Build a raw-to-report audit trail
body.text:
Keep the original export read-only where practical. Create a separate clean table, a rejection log and a derived session-summary table. Each row needs stable identifiers and a documented relationship to the other tables. A correction records original value, revised value, reason, date and responsible person. Avoid overwriting history merely to make the final spreadsheet look tidy.

For a synthetic pilot, use six paired session means: baseline 32,36,40,44,48,52 cm; retest 31,37,40,46,47,55 cm. Differences are−1,+1,0,+2,−1,+3 cm. These are already session means; do not invent trial-level precision that was not supplied. Create a separate clearly synthetic trial demonstration for invalid-trial handling if needed. Distinguish the real provenance of every table: observed, supplied, generated, corrected or derived.

body.heading: Analyze the pilot and explain its limitations
body.text:
The six synthetic differences sum to 4 cm, so mean bias is 4/6 ≈ 0.667 cm. Their sample variance is[(−1 − 2/3)²+(1 − 2/3)²+(0 − 2/3)²+(2 − 2/3)²+(−1 − 2/3)²+(3 − 2/3)²]/5 ≈ 2.667 cm². SD of differences is 1.633 cm and typical error is 1.633/√2 ≈ 1.155 cm under the equal-independent-error model.

Approximate limits of agreement are 0.667 ± 1.96 × 1.633, or about−2.534 to 3.867 cm. A conventional unbiased two-measurement error margin using that typical error is 1.96 × √2 × 1.155 ≈ 3.201 cm. Because the sample has a positive mean shift, investigate its source rather than silently assuming no bias. The six pairs are a teaching pilot, with substantial estimation uncertainty. Do not issue organization-wide individual action thresholds from this dataset.

body.heading: Defend your work against an unfamiliar change
body.text:
A reviewer now tells you that half the retests used a new software version, one operator changed encouragement, and the fastest athlete was missing because of travel. Your first task is to inspect the metadata and determine which comparisons remain interpretable. Do not simply add a limitation sentence while leaving an unjustified combined estimate unchanged.

Propose a repair proportional to the problem: reprocess comparable raw traces under one algorithm where possible, repeat staff instruction, analyze clearly labeled subsets when defensible, or collect a new baseline if comparability cannot be recovered. Report the uncertainty introduced by fewer observations. Explain which question the revised dataset can answer and which remains unresolved. A strong defence acknowledges a broken inference and repairs it; it does not defend every original output at all costs.

body.heading: Separate completion, competence and external assessment
body.text:
You can finish the readings and quizzes, complete a reproducible simulation, perform a supervised collection and pass an external defence at different times. Record these milestones separately. A self-marked exercise demonstrates engagement; it is not independent confirmation of measurement competence. The project needs review by a performance scientist who understands the chosen equipment and methods.

Submit the protocol, evidence trail, calculations, interpretation, presentation and revision log. Ask the reviewer to challenge event definitions, invalid-trial handling, assumptions, missingness and what action the evidence can support. Revise after feedback. If an athlete session or external reviewer is unavailable, label that component pending rather than declaring graduate or professional competence. The goal is an honest portfolio of demonstrated work that can grow as access and supervision improve.

body.heading: Run a cold reconstruction before the defence
body.text:
Give a colleague the inputs, protocol version and analysis instructions without your final report. Ask them to reconstruct one session mean and the paired-difference analysis. Differences reveal missing instructions, hidden spreadsheet selections or inconsistent rounding. Record what failed and repair the workflow before interpreting disagreement as an analyst’s lack of skill.

Then choose one result and trace it backward: report to derived table, derived table to included trials, and trials to the original record and validity decision. This is a practical audit of provenance. If you only have the supplied session means, stop the trace there and say that trial-level reconstruction is unavailable. A trustworthy portfolio makes the boundary of the evidence visible instead of filling gaps with invented detail.
